cards.front: Give one example of scarcity from your own week.

cards.back: the line between combinations of goods you *can* produce and ones you can't.
producing *on* the PPF, with no resources wasted.
each extra unit of a good costs more of the other good, which is why the PPF bows outward.
the opportunity cost of producing one more unit.
the benefit of consuming one more unit, measured by willingness to pay. It falls as you get more.
producing the mix of goods people value most, where MB = MC.
being able to produce something at a *lower opportunity cost* than others.
the PPF shifting outward, driven by capital accumulation and technological change.

cards.front: Why does the PPF bow outward instead of being a straight line?
Alex can make 4 pizzas or 2 cakes an hour; Sam can make 3 pizzas or 3 cakes. Who has the comparative advantage in cakes?
If MB > MC for the last unit produced, should the economy produce more or less? Why?
What does a point inside the PPF mean in real life?

cards.back: so many buyers and sellers that no one can influence the price.
a price measured against other goods. It's an Opportunity Cost.
other things equal, a higher price means a smaller quantity demanded.
other things equal, a higher price means a larger quantity supplied.
goods used *instead of* each other, versus goods used *together*.
demand rises with income, versus demand falls with income.
the price where quantity demanded = quantity supplied.
price above equilibrium means a surplus and the price falls; price below equilibrium means a shortage and the price rises.

cards.front: Coffee gets more expensive. What happens to demand for tea (a substitute) and for coffee creamer (a complement)?
A new technology cuts the cost of making phones. Which curve shifts, which way, and what happens to price and quantity?
Why does a price above equilibrium fall on its own?
Demand rises and supply falls at the same time. What do we know for sure?

cards.back:
= % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price (use the magnitude)
• **> 1: elastic** (quantity reacts a lot)
• **= 1: unit elastic**
• **< 1: inelastic** (quantity barely reacts)

= % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income
• Positive: **normal good** (> 1 income elastic, 0–1 income inelastic)
• Negative: **inferior good**

= % change in quantity of good A ÷ % change in price of good B
• Positive: **substitutes**
• Negative: **complements**
= % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price (ranges from 0, a vertical curve, to infinity, a horizontal curve)

cards.front: A 10% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 5%. Elastic or inelastic? What happens to total revenue?
Income rises 20% and bus rides fall 10%. What's the income elasticity, and what kind of good is it?
Why is the demand for gasoline more elastic over five years than over five days?
Hot dogs and buns: is the cross elasticity positive or negative?

cards.back: has consistent preferences and picks the best affordable bundle. Preferences are learned from *choices* (revealed preference, Samuelson), not from reading minds.
all bundles that use up the whole budget: P_M·Q_M + P_S·Q_S = Y.
the affordable area on and under the budget line.
price of one good in terms of the other. It is the (negative) slope of the budget line: −P_M/P_S.
combinations of goods that are equally good to the consumer. Higher curves are better ("more is better").
how much of one good you'd give up for one more of the other and still be equally happy. It's the slope of the indifference curve and measures marginal benefit.
curves get flatter as you move right, which reflects a preference for variety.

cards.front: Write the budget line for $60 income, $4 coffee, $6 muffin. What is its slope?

State the optimality condition in words and in symbols.
What do the indifference curves look like for perfect substitutes? For perfect complements?
Why is a bundle on the budget line but on a lower indifference curve not optimal?

cards.back: from Greek *anthropos* (human) + *logos* (study of).

• **Sociocultural**: social and cultural variation between societies
• **Linguistic**: how language shapes social life and culture
• **Archaeology**: the human past (and present) through **material remains**
• **Biological anthropology**: human biology and evolution, seen in a **biocultural** perspective (also called *physical anthropology*)
you can't understand one part (biology, culture, environment) without the whole.
compare across cultures, within cultures, across deep time, and with other primates.
understand a practice on its own culture's terms, without judging it by another culture's standards. Associated with Franz Boas.
shared, learned, social behaviour, or "the way we do things."
the physical traces of human activity.
objects people made or used / natural remains like food waste or seeds.

cards.front: How does the textbook define *anthropology*, *human* and *culture*?
Name the four fields of anthropology. What is *applied* anthropology?
What is another name for biological anthropology, and what areas fall under it?
Describe the three parts of the anthropological perspective.
Why have anthropologists been called "agents of colonialism," and what does decolonization mean for the field?
Why do anthropologists care so much about food practices?

cards.back: the science of classifying living things.
*Genus species* naming (e.g., *Homo sapiens*), from **Linnaeus** (*Systema Naturae*, 1735).
different tooth types (incisors, canines, premolars, molars), allowing a varied diet.
count of incisors.canines.premolars.molars in one quarter of the mouth.
able to grasp.
overlapping fields of view from forward-facing eyes, giving 3D depth perception.
sense of smell.
the moist, hairless nose pad of strepsirhines.
living in trees / on the ground.
active by day / at night / at irregular times.
evolutionary relationships between species, estimated using genetic differences and "molecular clocks."
last common ancestor.

cards.front: What are the distinguishing characteristics of primates?
What primates are strepsirhines, and what makes them unique?
How do New World and Old World monkeys differ? How did New World monkeys reach the Americas?
Name the two families of Hominoidea. Where do humans fit?
When did the first primates evolve?
True or false: today's non-human primates have been evolving for millions of years, just like us.
Keywords to define: taxonomic order, olfaction/rhinarium, dental formula, ontogeny, adaptive radiation.

cards.back: giving animals human traits. Traditionally avoided in science, but Frans de Waal argued that refusing to do it at all can make us miss real similarities. Do it consciously and critically.
the study of non-human primates (pioneers: **Jane Goodall** (chimps), **Dian Fossey** (gorillas), **Biruté Galdikas** (orangutans), all supported by Louis Leakey).
energy used at rest. Smaller animals have a higher BMR, so they need energy-rich food (insects, fruit, seeds; not leaves).
one sex leaves the birth group at maturity (usually males).
gestation length, interbirth interval, weaning age, maturity age, life expectancy.
aggressive or conflict behaviour.
friendly or bonding behaviour.
helping relatives, which indirectly passes on your own genes.
the period of sexual receptivity around ovulation.
few offspring, heavy investment in each (primates). *r-selection*: many offspring, little investment.
traits that evolve because they help win mates (big canines, a mandrill's colourful face).
understanding that others have their own beliefs and knowledge.
no strong hierarchy.
wild animals hunted for food, a major threat to primates.

cards.front: Why does studying non-human primates matter for human biology, evolution and primate advocacy?
What five aspects of behaviour do primatologists study, and why?
How would you use scientific evidence to counter the myth of Bigfoot?
Why does a behaviour need to vary *within* a subspecies, in the same kind of environment, to count as cultural?

cards.back: a testable, **falsifiable** proposed explanation. If it can't be proven wrong, it's a belief system.
a well-supported explanation backed by lots of evidence.
a conclusion from evidence plus reasoning.
(Plato) everything has a fixed, perfect "ideal" form.
(Aristotle) a fixed ladder of life from simple to complex.
nature is directed toward a purpose.
species never change (the medieval view).
(Hutton, then Lyell) the slow processes we see today worked the same way in the past, so Earth must be very old ("**deep time**").
(Cuvier) sudden disasters caused extinctions.
(John Ray) a group that can interbreed and produce **fertile offspring**.
small changes within a population over a few generations.
new species forming over long periods.
how successful an individual is at leaving offspring.
selection for traits that win mates.
a DNA segment coding for a molecule / one version of a gene / the gene's position on a chromosome.
genetic makeup / observable traits.
two identical alleles (RR, rr) / two different alleles (Rr).
slow steady change / long stability broken by bursts of change.

cards.front: Compare Lamarck's "transformational" evolution with Darwin's "variational" evolution. Why was Lamarck wrong?
How did Hutton and Lyell challenge traditional views?
What did Mendel contribute? What do we now call his "factors"?
Dominant vs. recessive; phenotype vs. genotype?
Which of mutation, gene flow, drift and selection is the only true source of **new** variation?
How does lactose tolerance show mutation and natural selection working together?
Keywords: sexual selection, gradualism, punctuated equilibrium, speciation, mass extinction.

cards.back: "the ability to think clearly and rationally about what to do or what to believe" (Lau, ch. 1).
reasoning about what to **believe**.
reasoning about what to **do**.
useful in any field, not just one subject.
the reasons, and the claim they're meant to support (see Unit 2 - Arguments and Standard Form).

cards.back: (declarative sentence) says that something is the case. It can be true or false, even if it's false or only an opinion. "Spot is a good dog" is a statement.
asks a question ("Is Spot a good dog?"). Not a statement.
gives a command ("Be a good dog, Spot"). Not a statement.
a set of statements, one of which (the conclusion) is supposed to be supported by the others (the premises).
words that flag which statements are which.
numbered premises, then the conclusion on the last line.
no logically possible situation where all premises are true and the conclusion is false.
not valid.
valid **and** all premises are actually true.
not sound (invalid, or has a false premise).

cards.front: Use the "It is true that..." test on: "Close the door", "Cats are reptiles", "Is it raining?". Which are statements?
Pick out the premises, conclusion, and indicators: "Since the lake froze, it must have been below zero, because water freezes at zero."
Put this in standard form: "Everyone in the club is a student. Priya is in the club. So Priya is a student."
Can an argument be valid and have a false conclusion? Can it be sound and have a false conclusion? Explain.
Why is "That statement is invalid" a category mistake?
In your own words, why does "the premises are true and the conclusion is true" *not* by itself make an argument valid?

cards.back: not contradictory. (A four-sided triangle is logically impossible. A flying gold mountain is logically possible, even if it breaks the laws of nature.)
a logically possible scenario where the premises are true and the conclusion is false.
the pattern left when you replace statements with variables (p, q, r).
a statement that's true no matter what (e.g. "Either it's raining or it's not").
premises: cannot all be true at the same time.
(as defined here) the conclusion is also one of the premises.
a *method* of arguing by showing the opposite leads to an absurdity.

cards.front: What exactly do you have to show to prove an argument is invalid?

Name the form: "If p then q. Not q. ∴ Not p." How is it different from denying the antecedent?
Is this valid? "If it snows, school is cancelled. School is cancelled. ∴ It snowed." (Hint: which form does this resemble, and can you build a counterexample?)
Why is "The moon is cheese. ∴ The moon is cheese" valid even though it's useless?
Explain in one sentence why an argument with inconsistent premises is always valid.
What are the steps of a reductio ad absurdum?

cards.back: asserts something ("He is here."). **This is a statement.**
asks a question ("Is he here?").
makes a request or gives a command ("Come here!").
any declarative sentence (a complete, grammatical sentence that makes a claim).

cards.front: Apply the "It is true that" test to: "Turn off the lights", "Penguins can swim", "Tomorrow's exam".

Give an example of a sentence that is both a statement and a command.

cards.back: (P, Q, R…) stand for statements.
the denial of Q ("It is not the case that Q").
a mistake in reasoning.
P or Q but *not both*.
P or Q *or both*. Default in this course: inclusive.
